output.content:
The street had moved overnight.

I know because I drew it myself yesterday, with a ruling pen and lamp oil on the skin of my wrist, and this morning the line is three houses east. 

It is the kind of lie a map will not tell you until you have lived with it. I was in the map room on the third floor of the Writers’ Building annex, where the Survey of India keeps its ink and its silence. Outside, the August rain had settled over Kolkata like a damp cloth. The fan above my table turned with a tired tick, tick, tick, pushing the smell of wet paper and camphor around the room.

My name is Meera Banerjee. I am twenty-nine, unmarried, and officially the draftsman’s assistant for Bengal’s northern wards. Unofficially, I am the only woman they will let handle the vellum because my hand does not shake. The men say it is because I was trained by my father, who mapped the tea gardens of Darjeeling before laudanum took him. They forget to say I am English-educated at Bethune and that I can read latitudes while my sari stays clean of ink.

Yesterday I surveyed Chitpur Road from the bridge to the ghats. The lane is called Katuri Gali in the ledgers, though the hawkers call it something else when they want brisk trade. It runs narrow between a copper-beating workshop and the red brick of the Marwari warehouse. I measured it with a chain and a theodolite borrowed from Mr. Hardwick, who pretends he does not know I am using it after hours. I inked it in at 2 a.m. under a kerosene lamp that made my shadow huge on the wall. I wrote the name carefully in Bengali and English, the two scripts side by side like reluctant cousins.

This morning the name is still there. The line is not.

I laid yesterday’s tracing beside today’s master sheet. The paper was still off the press, the cotton rag bright and cruel against the older work. On the tracing, Katuri Gali ran straight as a schoolboy’s ruler, hugging the river wall. On the master, where I had transferred it at first light, the same lane kinked eastward, as if it had shuffled in its sleep. The new line now cut through the back of the warehouse, through the courtyard of a house with a green veranda I have never seen on any municipal plan.

“Miss Banerjee?”

Mr. Hardwick stood in the doorway, the strap of his field case slung over his shoulder. He was fifty, or looked it, with a moustache gone white and a permanent squint from squinting at sextants. Rain had beaded on his hat.

“Mr. Hardwick. You’re late. The tide chart—”

“I saw your lamp under the door at five. Thought you’d be finished with Chitpur.” He stepped in, smelling of wet wool. “Let me see.”

I wanted to tell him it was a mistake, a slip of the ruling pen, a smear. Instead I pushed the two sheets toward him with a fingertip that trembled for the first time in years.

He frowned. He put on his spectacles. “You misdrew it.”

“No.” The word came out flat. I pointed. “Look. The warehouse wall. On the tracing it stops at the third pillar. On the master it cuts through.”

He bent closer. A bead of sweat rolled down his temple. “Maps do not move, Miss Banerjee.”

“Neither do streets.”

There was a pause. The fan ticked. Somewhere downstairs a peon was calling for chai.

Hardwick straightened. “You copied it wrong. Do it again. We need the final sheet for dinner at the Club. The Colonel wants the northern wards bound by Friday.”

He left me with the smell of rain on his coat. I sat alone with the two sheets and the rain hammering the shutters. I pulled out the field notebook. On 12 August I had sketched Katuri Gali with a pencil, then with ink, then checked it against the municipal list. It was consistent. Consistent and wrong this morning.

I took the ruler to the master sheet and measured. From the bridge abutment to the first turn: twenty-two millimetres on the tracing, twenty-nine on the master. Seven millimetres. At the scale we were using, that was thirty-six feet. An entire shopfront.

“Did you move it?” I asked the paper.

The paper did not answer.

I went to the washroom and splashed water on my face. In the mirror the lamp behind me painted my face gold. When I came back, the peon, Ratan, was there with tea in a tin cup, balancing it on a folded ledger.

“Mem sahib, you forgot the lamp.”

“I didn’t forget.”

He set the cup down. “The Babus in Chitpur say the lane is haunted. Old woman says it shifts when the tide is high.” He laughed, nervous. “They say the British drew the line wrong on purpose to tax the warehouse more.”

“Who told you that?”

“Everyone, Mem sahib. The boys who carry the chain.” He glanced at the sheets. “You should not draw that lane at night. The map room is for maps.”

I wanted to ask him what he meant, but Hardwick’s voice was already in my head: maps do not move. I told myself I had been working too long, that the monsoon light made me see things.

I locked the sheets in the metal cabinet and went home on foot through the rain. My quarters were above a printing press in Bowbazar, two rooms with a tin roof that sang when it rained. I had a cot, a desk, a stack of vellum, and a cat that belonged to the landlady.

On my desk lay the tracing I had taken at dawn. I remembered unrolling it when the light was thin and blue. I remembered the line being straight. I remembered, very clearly, the name Katuri Gali written at the top in my hand.

Now I looked again. In the right margin, in a pencil I did not recognize, there was a small notation: *moved again 13/8*. Under it, in my own hurried hand: *3 houses east*.

I did not write that.

The ink on the master sheet was still tacky. I pressed a finger to the line where Katuri Gali kinked. It came away damp. The damp was not from the room. The damp was warm.

I sat back. The rain had stopped. The press below had gone quiet. A fly buzzed against my window.

I had kept a habit from my father: every night I traced the day’s work onto a fresh sheet and locked the originals. It was a way of proving myself. It was also, I realized now, a way of watching.

I took the folio from the bottom of the cabinet, the one with the previous week’s Chitpur sheets. Night by night they told a small, terrible story. On the 9th, Katuri Gali sat where the municipal plan said it should. On the 10th, it had shifted a half-inch east. On the 11th, another. On the 12th, another. By the 13th, it had walked straight into the warehouse courtyard.

Each night the shift was small. Each night I had assumed it was my tired hand, or the paper stretching in the humidity. No one else saw the master sheets until the morning I would transfer them. No one else had the patience to compare.

The street was moving.

The cat jumped onto the desk and stared at the vellum. Its eyes were green in the lamplight. It stared not at me, but at the line where Katuri Gali ended, a line that now stopped just shy of the edge of my own window.

The floorboard creaked. I turned.

The door to my room was shut, as always. The bolt was on the inside. I had locked it when I came in.

Behind me, at the desk, the lamp flickered once, as if a breath had moved across it. The paper on the desk was blank for a heartbeat, then refilled.

On the master sheet, the street was moving again.
